results.title: mlf-core: a framework for deterministic machine learning | Bioinformatics | Oxford Academic
results.content: We applied mlf-core to develop deterministic models in various biomedical fields including a single-cell autoencoder with TensorFlow, a PyTorch-based U-Net model for liver-tumor segmentation in computed tomography scans, and a liver cancer classifier based on gene expression profiles with XGBoost. Additionally, mlf-core provides project templates and static code analysis (linting) functionality that ensures the sole usage of deterministic algorithms for GPU computing as well as setting all necessary random seeds for deterministic results. mlf-core provides a complete solution for deterministic ML that ensures deterministic model training and tackles other important aspects for determinism of the developed models, such as result visualization and hyperparameter tracking, operating system tracking, dependency management with containers, and a publicly hosted model documentation (Fig. 1). These templates include a minimal running example for training e.g. a convolutional neural network or a distributed gradient boosting model which meets a set of requirements that have been determined and empirically verified to enable deterministic ML model training on both the CPUs or GPUs. These requirements include the containerization of the runtime environment, the setting of all random seeds for all used libraries, the usage of solely deterministic algorithms, and the tracking of all hyperparameters and metrics. Additionally, three different training setups were tested: (i) A setup without specified seeds or any deterministic setting (*random*), (ii) a setup that specified random seeds for all libraries used for the model implementation (*seeds*), and (iii) a setup which specified all random seeds, and additionally forced deterministic algorithms together with disabled cuDNN benchmark functionality, as implemented in the mlf-core ecosystem (*deterministic*) (Supplementary Fig. S3). To evaluate the determinism of this model, we compared the loss values (log loss) among different runs with deterministic settings as provided by mlf-core, to the loss obtained from runs without deterministic settings. The mlf-core framework enforces all the aforementioned requirements for deterministic ML directly into the model code and thus provides the first complete solution for CPU and GPU reproducible ML (Supplementary Fig. S13). We showcased the usage of the mlf-core ecosystem to develop deterministic ML models for three different use cases relevant for biomedical data science.

results.title: How do you get a model to share the GPU and the CPU?
results.content: How do you get a model to share the GPU and the CPU? - High-Performance Computing / Machine Learning, LLMs, & AI - Level1Techs Forums. How do you get a model to share the GPU and the CPU? High-Performance ComputingMachine Learning, LLMs, & AI. I was very interested in how I could get the GPU and the CPU to share memory and computation. I am using Fedora with an AMD gpu (7900 XT 20 gigs of ram) on a system with 64 gigs of ram. * #### last reply [: wardtj Mar 2025](). #### replies. #### views. I am looking at LM studio with System Monitor running side by side expecting the GPU and CPU to be working hard and RAM usage nearing to max out on a larger model (unsloth DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama70B as per the video’s recommendation) but RAM usage CPU/GPU and Compute does not even go past 50%. I am also on Fedora and using LM Studio. I can use one or the other, but not both. I have 64GB of system RAM, a 7950X, and a 7900XTX (using ROCm). To use mixed CPU and GPU you need llama.cpp or any derivatives like Ollama. Well, ktransformers uses mixed inference as well, but its use case is more limited and needs more RAM than you have. You have to download llama.cpp executables, or build them from source. Then you launch its llama-server app with the relevant flags. --n-gpu-layers (or -ngl) followed by the number of layers to be loaded in GPU. The rest will go to system RAM. You need some trial and error to find the best fit and ‘watch -n 1 nvidia-smi’ will help you to monitor what’s happening. There are several parameters that interacts to use VRAM, -ngl -c -fa -ctk -ctv, so you need to experiment a little. With AMD you can use both ROCm or Vulkan. If you get the docker container for gpustack.ai and deploy that it will automatically balance layers between cpu and gpu. Need nvidia gpu for best and easiest config. ### New & Unread Topics.
